svg.title: Atmospheric stability: stable and unstable air
svg.desc: Two panels. Stable air resists vertical motion: small vertical disturbances dampen out and disappear, and cool dry air brings good, generally clear weather. Unstable air lets small vertical movements grow, causing turbulent airflow, convective activity, extensive vertical clouds and severe weather, most of all when the air is moist and warm. A bar chart of lapse rates per 1,000 feet: average 2 degrees C, dry adiabatic 3 degrees C, moist adiabatic 1.1 to 2.8 degrees C. Cards describe temperature inversions: the top acts as a lid, and high humidity can produce clouds, fog, haze or smoke with diminished visibility.
svg.text: Atmospheric stability: stable and unstable air
The stability of the atmosphere depends on its ability to resist vertical motion. The combination of
moisture and temperature determines the stability of the air and the resulting weather.
Stable air
A small vertical push
dies out as the parcel is
resisted: smooth air
Makes vertical movement difficult; small vertical
disturbances dampen out and disappear
Cool, dry air is very stable and resists vertical
movement, which leads to good and generally clear
weather
Inversion layers: shallow layers of smooth,
stable air close to the ground
Unstable air
Small movements grow
larger: tall clouds
and turbulence
Small vertical air movements tend to become
larger, resulting in turbulent airflow and
convective activity
Can lead to significant turbulence, extensive
vertical clouds and severe weather
Greatest when the air is moist and warm: tropical
regions in summer see thunderstorms on a daily
basis
Lapse rate: how fast temperature falls as air rises (per 1,000 feet)
Average, ascending air
Dry adiabatic (unsaturated)
Moist adiabatic
Moist air cools at a slower rate, so it is generally less stable than dry air: it must rise higher before its
temperature cools to that of the surrounding air. Bars are drawn in °C; the moist bar spans its stated range.
Inversion: temperature rises with altitude
The top of the layer acts as a lid, keeping weather
and pollutants trapped below
High relative humidity can form clouds, fog, haze
or smoke, diminishing visibility in the layer
Two kinds of inversion
Surface-based: on clear, cool nights the air within
a few hundred feet of the ground becomes cooler
than the air above it
Frontal: warm air spreads over a layer of cooler
air, or cooler air is forced under warmer air
